*   The criterion for separation and attachment lines is based on Kenwright et al. [KHL99] (cited in [S1, unofficial]).

The claim states that the criterion for separation and attachment lines is based on Kenwright et al. [KHL99]. The provided text from Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Crease lines on crease surfaces are related to separation and attachment lines on general surfaces in vector fields. The criterion by Kenwright et al. [KHL99] defines separation and attachment lines as locations, where the projected flow field on a mesh is parallel to one of the projected Jacobian’s real eigenvectors.' This confirms that the text cites Kenwright et al. [KHL99] as the basis for the definition/criterion of these lines.

*   **Strengths:** Numerically stable in areas of ambiguous convexity where the gradient has a distinct and consistent direction [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method is 'numerically stable in areas of ambiguous convexity where the gradient has a distinct and consistent direction'. This is directly supported by the text in Source [S1], which explicitly contrasts the proposed approach with flow-based integration (which is 'numerically unstable due to substantially varying gradient directions'). The text states: 'Unlike flow-based surface integration which is numerically unstable due to substantially varying gradient directions close to separation structures, this approach uses constrained gradient-based integration only in areas of ambiguous convexity where the gradient has a distinct and consistent direction.'
